# Research sources

<!-- Generated by scripts/skill_library.py from data/research.json. Do not edit by hand. -->

Each citation (authors, year, title, venue) was confirmed to exist by web search on the check date. Volume and page numbers are omitted throughout. On the same date the abstract or summary page of as many sources as possible was fetched and the stored finding was corrected against it; the field finding_checked_against says, per source, whether that check was against the paper's own abstract or text, against a secondary summary, or not done. No full text was read end to end, so read the source before relying on a specific number.

Of 181 sources, the finding was checked against the paper's own abstract or text for 58, against a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page) for 25, and against nothing for 98. Each entry says which.

Weight says how much a source can bear when deciding what a caregiver does at home with a child of 4-6: `strong`, `moderate` or `weak`. It is this project's judgement, not a rating taken from the source. For the synthesis by area, read [research-base.md](research-base.md).

## Cross-cutting

### `bailey-2020`

Bailey, D. H., Duncan, G. J., Cunha, F., Foorman, B. R., & Yeager, D. S. (2020). Persistence and fade-out of educational-intervention effects: Mechanisms and potential solutions. Psychological Science in the Public Interest. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7787577/)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 0 mo to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Effects of early interventions on the skills they target usually shrink after the intervention ends. Persistence is more likely when later environments keep building on the skill, or when the intervention changes something that would not have developed anyway.
- Limits: A review of mechanisms, and the explanation for fade-out is still debated. It concerns programs, not a parent's sustained routine.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `alfieri-2011`

Alfieri, L., Brooks, P. J., Aldrich, N. J., & Tenenbaum, H. R. (2011). Does discovery-based instruction enhance learning? Journal of Educational Psychology. [Link](https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ933606)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 4 y to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across 164 studies, explicit instruction beat unassisted discovery (d = 0.38), and enhanced discovery with guidance, feedback or worked examples beat other forms of instruction (d = 0.30).
- Limits: Most studies involved older children and adults, not preschoolers.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: science.

### `weisberg-2016`

Weisberg, D. S., Hirsh-Pasek, K., Golinkoff, R. M., Kittredge, A. K., & Klahr, D. (2016). Guided play: Principles and practices. Current Directions in Psychological Science. [Link](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0963721416645512)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 8 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Guided play keeps the child in control of the action while an adult chooses the materials and steers attention toward a learning goal with questions and hints.
- Limits: A short position review by proponents of the approach.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: science, building.

### `skene-2022`

Skene, K., O'Farrelly, C. M., Byrne, E. M., Kirby, N., Stevens, E. C., & Ramchandani, P. G. (2022). Can guidance during play enhance children's learning and development in educational contexts? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Child Development. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35018635/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 12 mo to 8 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Compared with direct instruction, guided play gave better results for early maths, shape knowledge and task switching. Compared with free play, it gave better spatial vocabulary.
- Limits: 39 studies with few per outcome, mostly in classrooms. Direct instruction was not worse on most outcomes.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: math, building, science.

### `lillard-2013`

Lillard, A. S., Lerner, M. D., Hopkins, E. J., Dore, R. A., Smith, E. D., & Palmquist, C. M. (2013). The impact of pretend play on children's development: A review of the evidence. Psychological Bulletin. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22905949/)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 2 y to 8 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Existing evidence does not support strong causal claims that pretend play drives creativity, intelligence, problem solving, theory of mind or self-regulation. It may be one of several routes to those outcomes, or a by-product.
- Limits: The conclusion is about the weakness of the evidence, not proof that pretend play does nothing. A later trial of structured drama games found a specific benefit (`goldstein-2018`).
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `romeo-2018`

Romeo, R. R., Leonard, J. A., Robinson, S. T., West, M. R., Mackey, A. P., Rowe, M. L., & Gabrieli, J. D. E. (2018). Beyond the 30-million-word gap: Children's conversational exposure is associated with language-related brain function. Psychological Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5945324)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 4 y to 6 y 11 mo. Weight: weak.
- Finding: In 36 children aged 4-6, the number of adult-child conversational turns, not the number of adult words heard, was related to verbal scores and to activation in language areas, independent of family income and education.
- Limits: Small and correlational. Talkative children may draw more turns from adults.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: reading.

### `hidi-renninger-2006`

Hidi, S., & Renninger, K. A. (2006). The four-phase model of interest development. Educational Psychologist. [Link](https://works.swarthmore.edu/fac-education/12)

- Design: theory. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Interest develops in four phases: triggered situational interest, maintained situational interest, emerging individual interest and well-developed individual interest. Early phases depend on outside support from people and materials.
- Limits: A model, not a test.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `gullich-2022`

Güllich, A., Macnamara, B. N., & Hambrick, D. Z. (2022). What makes a champion? Early multidisciplinary practice, not early specialization, predicts world-class performance. Perspectives on Psychological Science. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34260336/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 6 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Pooling studies of athletes, adult world-class performers had more childhood practice across several sports and specialised later than national-level performers, who did more early sport-specific practice.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date. Retrospective reports by elite athletes.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: movement.

### `deloache-2007`

DeLoache, J. S., Simcock, G., & Macari, S. (2007). Planes, trains, automobiles - and tea sets: Extremely intense interests in very young children. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18020834/)

- Design: observational. Ages studied: 12 mo to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Surveys and interviews with 177 parents found that nearly a third of young children have an extremely intense interest in a category such as vehicles or dinosaurs, much more often boys.
- Limits: Parent report. Describes interests; says nothing about outcomes.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `shah-2018`

Shah, P. E., Weeks, H. M., Richards, B., & Kaciroti, N. (2018). Early childhood curiosity and kindergarten reading and math academic achievement. Pediatric Research. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29884846/)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In about 6,200 US children, higher parent-reported curiosity was associated with higher kindergarten reading and math scores, more so for children from low-income families.
- Limits: Correlational.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: science.

### `macnamara-2014`

Macnamara, B. N., Hambrick, D. Z., & Oswald, F. L. (2014). Deliberate practice and performance in music, games, sports, education, and professions: A meta-analysis. Psychological Science. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24986855/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 6 y to 75 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Deliberate practice explained about 21% of the differences in music performance, 18% in sports, 26% in games, 4% in education and under 1% in professions. The authors conclude it is important, but not as important as has been argued.
- Limits: Mostly older learners and adults.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: music, movement.

### `mahoney-2006`

Mahoney, J. L., Harris, A. L., & Eccles, J. S. (2006). Organized activity participation, positive youth development, and the over-scheduling hypothesis. Social Policy Report. [Link](https://www.srcd.org/sites/default/files/documents/2006_4_sprbrief_mahoney.pdf)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 5 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Young people aged 5-18 who took part in organised activities did better on achievement and school completion than those who did not; only a small minority were heavily scheduled, and evidence of harm from over-scheduling was weak.
- Limits: Read from a policy brief. Correlational; previous work suggests diminishing returns at very high participation.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `jirout-klahr-2012`

Jirout, J., & Klahr, D. (2012). Children's scientific curiosity: In search of an operational definition of an elusive concept. Developmental Review. [Link](https://kilthub.cmu.edu/articles/journal_contribution/Children_s_scientific_curiosity_In_search_of_an_operational_definition_of_an_elusive_concept/6613916/1)

- Design: theory. Ages studied: 3 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Defined curiosity as the level of uncertainty a child prefers before exploring, and proposed a preschool measure of it.
- Limits: A definition and measure, not an intervention.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: science.

### `alexander-2012`

Alexander, J. M., Johnson, K. E., & Kelley, K. (2012). Longitudinal analysis of the relations between opportunities to learn about science and the development of interests related to science. Science Education. [Link](https://zendy.io/title/10.1002/sce.21018)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 3 y to 7 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Children's early interest in science-related topics was sustained when families supplied opportunities to learn about it, such as books, visits and conversation.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Small sample.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: science.

## Reading

### `nelp-2008`

National Early Literacy Panel. (2008). Developing early literacy: Report of the National Early Literacy Panel. National Institute for Literacy. [Link](https://www.nichd.nih.gov/publications/pubs/Documents/NELPReport09.pdf)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 0 mo to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across roughly 300 studies, the strongest preschool predictors of later decoding, spelling and comprehension were alphabet knowledge, phonological awareness, rapid naming, writing or name writing, and phonological memory. Code-focused teaching improved those skills. Shared reading mainly improved oral language.
- Limits: The predictors are correlational. Most intervention studies were short and school based.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: writing.

### `castles-2018`

Castles, A., Rastle, K., & Nation, K. (2018). Ending the reading wars: Reading acquisition from novice to expert. Psychological Science in the Public Interest. [Link](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/publications/ending-the-reading-wars-reading-acquisition-from-novice-to-expert.html)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 4 y to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Systematic phonics is necessary for learning to decode an alphabetic script but is not sufficient. Fluent word reading also needs a large amount of reading experience, and comprehension depends on vocabulary and knowledge of the world.
- Limits: A narrative review, mostly about school instruction.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `ies-foundational-2016`

Foorman, B., Beyler, N., Borradaile, K., Coyne, M., Denton, C. A., Dimino, J., et al. (2016). Foundational skills to support reading for understanding in kindergarten through 3rd grade (NCEE 2016-4008). What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences. [Link](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/21)

- Design: evidence-guide. Ages studied: 5 y to 8 y 11 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Four recommendations: teach academic language (minimal evidence), teach awareness of speech sounds and letter-sound links (strong), teach decoding and word analysis (strong), and have children read connected text every day for accuracy, fluency and comprehension (moderate).
- Limits: Written for kindergarten to grade 3 classrooms. A younger child who already decodes is outside the studied population by age, though not by skill.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `share-1995`

Share, D. L. (1995). Phonological recoding and self-teaching: Sine qua non of reading acquisition. Cognition. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7789090/)

- Design: theory. Ages studied: 5 y to 12 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Self-teaching hypothesis: each time a child successfully sounds out a new word, that is a learning trial that builds the word-specific memory needed for fluent reading. Decoding skill plus reading volume drives growth.
- Limits: A theoretical review. Later experiments support it, but it does not prescribe a home routine.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `ehri-2014`

Ehri, L. C. (2014). Orthographic mapping in the acquisition of sight word reading, spelling memory, and vocabulary learning. Scientific Studies of Reading. [Link](https://www.readingrockets.org/research-by-topic/orthographic-mapping-acquisition-sight-word-reading-spelling-memory-and-vocabulary)

- Design: theory. Ages studied: 4 y to 12 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Words become readable at sight when their spellings are bonded to their pronunciations and meanings. That bonding needs phonemic awareness and letter-sound knowledge, and spelling and reading draw on the same knowledge.
- Limits: A theory paper summarising the author's research program.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: writing.

### `mol-2008`

Mol, S. E., Bus, A. G., de Jong, M. T., & Smeets, D. J. H. (2008). Added value of dialogic parent-child book readings: A meta-analysis. Early Education and Development. [Link](https://www.scinapse.io/papers/2088476022)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 2 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 16 studies, training parents in dialogic reading improved children's expressive vocabulary more than ordinary reading aloud. The effect was clearly smaller for 4-5-year-olds than for 2-3-year-olds, and smaller for children at risk.
- Limits: Short-term vocabulary outcomes. For a child near 5, the gain from questioning style alone is modest.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `senechal-2002`

Senechal, M., & LeFevre, J.-A. (2002). Parental involvement in the development of children's reading skill: A five-year longitudinal study. Child Development. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11949902)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y to 8 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 168 children followed from kindergarten to grade 3, storybook exposure predicted vocabulary and listening comprehension, which predicted grade 3 reading. Parents teaching letters and words predicted early literacy skills and grade 1 reading. The two paths were largely separate.
- Limits: Correlational, in middle-class Canadian families.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `wwc-prek-2022`

What Works Clearinghouse. (2022). Preparing young children for school (WWC 2022009). Institute of Education Sciences. [Link](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/practiceguide/30)

- Design: evidence-guide. Ages studied: 3 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Seven recommendations for preschool programs covering social-emotional skills, executive function, mathematical ideas and math talk, letters and sounds, shared book reading and vocabulary.
- Limits: The recommendation list is summarised from memory and was not re-read on the check date. Evidence levels differ by recommendation. Classroom setting.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: math, social-emotional.

### `suggate-2013`

Suggate, S. P., Schaughency, E. A., & Reese, E. (2013). Children learning to read later catch up to children reading earlier. Early Childhood Research Quarterly. [Link](https://stmichaelsteiner.hounslow.sch.uk/wp-content/uploads/2019/12/Children-learning-to-read-later-catch-up-to-children-reading-earlier.pdf)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 5 y to 11 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: New Zealand children taught to read from age 5 were ahead at first on letter naming, word and passage reading, but children taught from age 7 caught up by age 11, and in a second sample the later starters had somewhat better reading comprehension.
- Limits: Non-experimental; families chose the schools. The authors urge further research.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `mol-bus-2011`

Mol, S. E., & Bus, A. G. (2011). To read or not to read: A meta-analysis of print exposure from infancy to early adulthood. Psychological Bulletin. [Link](https://www.scinapse.io/papers/2023991700)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 0 mo to 25 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across 99 studies, the amount of reading done for pleasure was associated with comprehension, vocabulary and spelling at every age, and the association grew stronger with age.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date. Correlational; good readers read more.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `ehri-2001`

Ehri, L. C., Nunes, S. R., Stahl, S. A., & Willows, D. M. (2001). Systematic phonics instruction helps students learn to read: Evidence from the National Reading Panel's meta-analysis. Review of Educational Research. [Link](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.3102/00346543071003393)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 5 y to 12 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Systematic phonics instruction improved reading more than unsystematic or no phonics, with the largest effects when it began in kindergarten or first grade.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `dowdall-2020`

Dowdall, N., Melendez-Torres, G. J., Murray, L., Gardner, F., Hartford, L., & Cooper, P. J. (2020). Shared picture book reading interventions for child language development: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Child Development. [Link](https://centaur.reading.ac.uk/80756)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 12 mo to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Interventions that train adults in shared picture-book reading improved children's expressive and receptive language, with smaller effects for older children.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the repository page blocked automated reading.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `cheatham-allor-2012`

Cheatham, J. P., & Allor, J. H. (2012). The influence of decodability in early reading text on reading achievement: A review of the evidence. Reading and Writing. [Link](https://www.readingrockets.org/resources/resource-library/influence-decodability-early-reading-text-reading-achievement-review)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 5 y to 8 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Decodability is a critical feature of early reading text and brings immediate benefits, especially for accuracy, but early texts should be chosen on several criteria, not decodability alone.
- Limits: Read from a summary page. Few direct comparisons exist.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `noble-2019`

Noble, C., Sala, G., Peter, M., Lingwood, J., Rowland, C., Gobet, F., & Pine, J. (2019). The impact of shared book reading on children's language skills: A meta-analysis. Educational Research Review. [Link](https://livrepository.liverpool.ac.uk/3054189/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 12 mo to 8 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Shared book reading interventions had a small effect on language (g = 0.19), smaller than earlier meta-analyses reported. Against active control groups the effect was near zero (g = 0.03), and it was not significant at follow-up.
- Limits: The size of the effect depends on what the comparison group did.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

## Writing

### `ouellette-2017`

Ouellette, G., & Senechal, M. (2017). Invented spelling in kindergarten as a predictor of reading and spelling in Grade 1: A new pathway to literacy, or just the same road, less known? Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://www.readingrockets.org/research-by-topic/invented-spelling-kindergarten-predictor-reading-and-spelling-grade-1)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 5 y to 7 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In about 170 kindergartners, how sophisticated a child's invented spellings were predicted grade 1 reading and spelling over and above phonological awareness and letter knowledge.
- Limits: Longitudinal, not experimental. The authors' separate training studies are not reviewed here.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: reading.

### `ies-writers-2012`

Graham, S., Bollinger, A., Booth Olson, C., D'Aoust, C., MacArthur, C., McCutchen, D., & Olinghouse, N. (2012). Teaching elementary school students to be effective writers (NCEE 2012-4058). What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences. [Link](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/17)

- Design: evidence-guide. Ages studied: 5 y to 11 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Provide daily time to write (minimal evidence). Teach the writing process and writing for different purposes (strong). Teach handwriting, spelling, sentence construction and typing until fluent (moderate). Build a community of writers (minimal).
- Limits: Elementary classrooms. Preschool is out of scope.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `santangelo-2016`

Santangelo, T., & Graham, S. (2016). A comprehensive meta-analysis of handwriting instruction. Educational Psychology Review. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-015-9335-1)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 5 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Explicit handwriting instruction improved legibility and fluency, and also improved the quality and length of what students wrote.
- Limits: School-age samples, starting at kindergarten.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `puranik-2011`

Puranik, C. S., & Lonigan, C. J. (2011). From scribbles to scrabble: Preschool children's developing knowledge of written language. Reading and Writing. [Link](https://link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s11145-009-9220-8)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 3 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 372 preschoolers, writing knowledge developed in a consistent order: general features of writing first, then letters and name writing, then spelling. Name writing was the most advanced skill at each age.
- Limits: Descriptive. It shows a typical order, not what teaching changes.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `grissmer-2010`

Grissmer, D., Grimm, K. J., Aiyer, S. M., Murrah, W. M., & Steele, J. S. (2010). Fine motor skills and early comprehension of the world: Two new school readiness indicators. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20822219/)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y to 11 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Across three large longitudinal datasets, fine motor skill and general knowledge at kindergarten entry predicted later math and reading over and above early math, reading and attention.
- Limits: Correlational. It does not show that training fine motor skill raises achievement.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: art, cross-cutting.

### `graham-hebert-2011`

Graham, S., & Hebert, M. (2011). Writing to read: A meta-analysis of the impact of writing and writing instruction on reading. Harvard Educational Review. [Link](https://asu.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/writing-to-read-a-meta-analysis-of-the-impact-of-writing-and-writ/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 6 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In true and quasi-experiments, writing about material read improved comprehension of it, and teaching writing improved reading comprehension, fluency and word reading.
- Limits: School-age students; ages are not given in the abstract read.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: reading.

### `senechal-2012`

Sénéchal, M., Ouellette, G., Pagan, S., & Lever, R. (2012). The role of invented spelling on learning to read in low-phoneme awareness kindergartners: A randomized-control-trial study. Reading and Writing. [Link](https://ir.library.carleton.ca/pub/11882)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 5 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: 56 kindergartners with weak phoneme awareness were randomly assigned to 16 small-group sessions over eight weeks. Children who practised invented spelling with feedback learned to read more words than children given phoneme-segmentation training or storybook reading.
- Limits: Small, and limited to children who started with weak phoneme awareness.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: reading.

### `ouellette-2008`

Ouellette, G., & Sénéchal, M. (2008). Pathways to literacy: A study of invented spelling and its role in learning to read. Child Development. [Link](https://www.readingrockets.org/research-by-topic/invented-spelling-kindergarten-predictor-reading-and-spelling-grade-1)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 5 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Five-year-olds who practised invented spelling with feedback learned to read more words than those given phonological-awareness training or drawing.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page checked on the check date was for a different paper by the same authors. Small sample.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: reading.

### `james-2012`

James, K. H., & Engelhardt, L. (2012). The effects of handwriting experience on functional brain development in pre-literate children. Trends in Neuroscience and Education. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4274624)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 4 y to 5 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Pre-literate 4- and 5-year-olds who practised printing letters, but not those who traced or typed them, later showed adult-like activation in reading-related brain areas when viewing letters.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Very small, brain imaging only.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: reading.

### `hall-2015`

Hall, A. H., Simpson, A., Guo, Y., & Wang, S. (2015). Examining the effects of preschool writing instruction on emergent literacy skills: A systematic review of the literature. Literacy Research and Instruction. [Link](https://tigerprints.clemson.edu/eugene_pubs/41)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Writing instruction in preschool, including guided invented spelling and name writing, improved emergent literacy skills such as letter knowledge and phonological awareness.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Few studies.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

## Math

### `duncan-2007`

Duncan, G. J., Dowsett, C. J., Claessens, A., Magnuson, K., Huston, A. C., Klebanov, P., et al. (2007). School readiness and later achievement. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18020822/)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y 6 mo to 14 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across six longitudinal datasets, math skill at school entry was the strongest predictor of later achievement, followed by reading and attention. Social-emotional behaviour at entry did not predict later achievement.
- Limits: Correlational with extensive controls. The causal effect of boosting early math is likely smaller than the correlation (see bailey-2020).
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: reading, cross-cutting.

### `siegler-2008`

Siegler, R. S., & Ramani, G. B. (2008). Playing linear numerical board games promotes low-income children's numerical development. Developmental Science. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18801120/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 4 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Low-income preschoolers who played a linear number board game for four 15-minute sessions caught up with more affluent peers in number-line estimation; a version with colours instead of numbers did not help.
- Limits: Head Start samples. A child with strong number knowledge may already be at ceiling on a 1-10 board.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `ramani-2008`

Ramani, G. B., & Siegler, R. S. (2008). Promoting broad and stable improvements in low-income children's numerical knowledge through playing number board games. Child Development. [Link](https://drum.lib.umd.edu/handle/1903/10061)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 4 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Replicated the board-game effect on four tasks: number-line estimation, magnitude comparison, counting and numeral identification. Gains were still present nine weeks later. Children's reported board-game play at home was related to their number knowledge.
- Limits: Head Start samples and a short follow-up.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `ies-math-2013`

Frye, D., Baroody, A. J., Burchinal, M., Carver, S. M., Jordan, N. C., & McDowell, J. (2013). Teaching math to young children (NCEE 2014-4005). What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences. [Link](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/18)

- Design: evidence-guide. Ages studied: 3 y to 6 y 11 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Teach number and operations along a developmental progression (moderate evidence). Teach geometry, patterns, measurement and data (minimal). Monitor progress (minimal). Teach children to describe their world mathematically (minimal). Give math dedicated time each day and weave it through the day (minimal).
- Limits: Classroom guide for ages 3-6. Only the first recommendation has more than minimal evidence.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: building.

### `berkowitz-2015`

Berkowitz, T., Schaeffer, M. W., Maloney, E. A., Peterson, L., Gregor, C., Levine, S. C., & Beilock, S. L. (2015). Math at home adds up to achievement in school. Science. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26450209/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 6 y to 7 y 6 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 587 first-graders, families given an app of short math story problems to do together saw more math growth across the school year than families given a reading app, most of all when the parents were anxious about math.
- Limits: First grade, not preschool. A published comment questioned the analysis; it appeared in search results and was not reviewed.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `levine-2010`

Levine, S. C., Suriyakham, L. W., Rowe, M. L., Huttenlocher, J., & Gunderson, E. A. (2010). What counts in the development of young children's number knowledge? Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2998540)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 14 mo to 3 y 10 mo. Weight: weak.
- Finding: The amount of number talk parents used between 14 and 30 months predicted children's understanding of cardinal number at 46 months, controlling for socioeconomic status and other talk.
- Limits: 44 families, correlational, toddler years.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `clements-2011`

Clements, D. H., & Sarama, J. (2011). Early childhood mathematics intervention. Science. [Link](https://researchconnect.buffalo.edu/en/publications/early-childhood-mathematics-intervention/)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 6 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Preschool math programs built on learning trajectories raise math achievement, including for low-income children. Early math is broader than counting and includes space, shape and pattern.
- Limits: A review written by the developers of one such curriculum.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: building.

### `jordan-2009`

Jordan, N. C., Kaplan, D., Ramineni, C., & Locuniak, M. N. (2009). Early math matters: Kindergarten number competence and later mathematics outcomes. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2782699)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 5 y 6 mo to 9 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 378 Delaware kindergartners (196 followed to third grade), number competence in kindergarten strongly predicted math achievement and its growth through third grade.
- Limits: Correlational. Low-income children were more often missing at the last wave.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `watts-2014`

Watts, T. W., Duncan, G. J., Siegler, R. S., & Davis-Kean, P. E. (2014). What's past is prologue: Relations between early mathematics knowledge and high school achievement. Educational Researcher. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4719158)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y 6 mo to 15 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In a national US sample, math ability at 54 months predicted math achievement at age 15, and growth in math between 54 months and first grade predicted it even more strongly.
- Limits: Non-experimental; the authors flag omitted-variable bias.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `daucourt-2021`

Daucourt, M. C., Napoli, A. R., Quinn, J. M., Wood, S. G., & Hart, S. A. (2021). The home math environment and math achievement: A meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8634776)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 2 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across many studies, home math activities had a small positive association with children's math achievement, with direct number activities more strongly related than indirect ones such as cooking or board games.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date. Correlational.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `maloney-2015`

Maloney, E. A., Ramirez, G., Gunderson, E. A., Levine, S. C., & Beilock, S. L. (2015). Intergenerational effects of parents' math anxiety on children's math achievement and anxiety. Psychological Science. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26253552/)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 6 y to 8 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: First and second graders learned less math over a school year, and became more math-anxious, when their math-anxious parents helped often with math homework.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date. Correlational.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `rittle-johnson-2017`

Rittle-Johnson, B., Fyfe, E. R., Hofer, K. G., & Farran, D. C. (2017). Early math trajectories: Low-income children's mathematics knowledge from ages 4 to 11. Child Development. [Link](https://dreme.stanford.edu/publication/early-math-trajectories-low-income-childrens-mathematics-knowledge-from-ages-4-to-11/)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y to 11 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 517 low-income US children, preschool knowledge of quantities, counting and repeating patterns predicted fifth-grade math. By the end of first grade, linking numerals to quantities, calculation and patterning were the important predictors.
- Limits: Read from a summary listing. Correlational; one low-income sample.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `bailey-2014`

Bailey, D. H., Watts, T. W., Littlefield, A. K., & Geary, D. C. (2014). State and trait effects on individual differences in children's mathematical development. Psychological Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4292922)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 6 y to 15 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In two datasets, stable traits of the child explained much more of the year-to-year continuity in math achievement than the direct effect of earlier math knowledge, so correlations between early and later math overstate how much an early boost carries forward.
- Limits: Statistical modelling of observational data.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: cross-cutting.

## Science

### `bonawitz-2011`

Bonawitz, E., Shafto, P., Gweon, H., Goodman, N. D., Spelke, E., & Schulz, L. (2011). The double-edged sword of pedagogy: Instruction limits spontaneous exploration and discovery. Cognition. [Link](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/60992)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 4 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Preschoolers who were shown one function of a new toy by a teacher explored it less and found fewer of its other functions than children who were not directly taught.
- Limits: One toy, one session, a museum sample. It shows a cost of demonstration for exploration, not that instruction is harmful in general.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `gopnik-2012`

Gopnik, A. (2012). Scientific thinking in young children: Theoretical advances, empirical research, and policy implications. Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3422420)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 2 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Preschoolers test hypotheses, learn from patterns in data and from their own interventions, and infer causes in ways that resemble scientific reasoning. Exploratory play serves this.
- Limits: A review of lab studies by a leading proponent. It does not test home activities.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `chouinard-2007`

Chouinard, M. M. (2007). Children's questions: A mechanism for cognitive development. Monographs of the Society for Research in Child Development. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17394580/)

- Design: observational. Ages studied: 12 mo to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Preschoolers ask adults a very large number of information-seeking questions, usually get informative answers, and keep asking when they do not. With age the questions shift from facts toward explanations.
- Limits: Observational: a small number of recorded children plus diary studies.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: cross-cutting.

### `klahr-nigam-2004`

Klahr, D., & Nigam, M. (2004). The equivalence of learning paths in early science instruction: Effects of direct instruction and discovery learning. Psychological Science. [Link](https://www.cmu.edu/dietrich/psychology/pdf/klahr/PDFs/KlahrNigam.PsychSci.pdf)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 8 y to 10 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: 112 third and fourth graders were randomly assigned to learn how to design a fair experiment by direct instruction or by discovery. 77% of the direct-instruction group mastered it against 23% of the discovery group, and masters from either route did equally well on a later transfer task.
- Limits: Older children; one skill.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `legare-2014`

Legare, C. H. (2014). The contributions of explanation and exploration to children's scientific reasoning. Child Development Perspectives. [Link](https://cacs-dev.squarespace.com/s/the-contributions-of-explanation-and-exploration-to-childrens-scientic-reasoning.pdf)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: When preschoolers are asked to explain an outcome that surprised them, they go on to explore in ways that test their explanation, and they learn more about the cause.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Based mainly on the author's lab studies.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `schulz-bonawitz-2007`

Schulz, L. E., & Bonawitz, E. B. (2007). Serious fun: Preschoolers engage in more exploratory play when evidence is confounded. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://cocosci.dreamhosters.com/Liz/SchulzBonawitzInPress.pdf)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 4 y to 5 y 10 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: 64 preschoolers (average age 4 years 9 months) kept playing with a familiar toy rather than a new one when what they had seen left it unclear how the toy worked; when it was clear, they preferred the new toy.
- Limits: Checked against an author manuscript. Museum visitors; one toy.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `morgan-2016`

Morgan, P. L., Farkas, G., Hillemeier, M. M., & Maczuga, S. (2016). Science achievement gaps begin very early, persist, and are largely explained by modifiable factors. Educational Researcher. [Link](https://pure.psu.edu/en/publications/science-achievement-gaps-begin-very-early-persist-and-are-largely/)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 5 y to 14 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In 7,757 US children followed from kindergarten to eighth grade, science gaps visible by third grade persisted, and were largely explained by general knowledge of the world, reading and math at kindergarten entry.
- Limits: Correlational.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `frazier-2009`

Frazier, B. N., Gelman, S. A., & Wellman, H. M. (2009). Preschoolers' search for explanatory information within adult-child conversation. Child Development. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2784636)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 2 y to 5 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In everyday transcripts and an experiment with 42 children aged 3-5, children who got a real explanation to a 'why' or 'how' question agreed or asked a follow-up; children who got a non-answer repeated the question or offered their own explanation.
- Limits: Small samples.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: cross-cutting.

### `crowley-2001`

Crowley, K., Callanan, M. A., Tenenbaum, H. R., & Allen, E. (2001). Parents explain more often to boys than to girls during shared scientific thinking. Psychological Science. [Link](https://eprints.kingston.ac.uk/253/)

- Design: observational. Ages studied: 12 mo to 8 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: At interactive science museum exhibits, parents gave explanations about three times as often to boys as to girls.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the repository page had no abstract. Museum visits only.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

## Art

### `winner-2013`

Winner, E., Goldstein, T. R., & Vincent-Lancrin, S. (2013). Art for art's sake? The impact of arts education. OECD Publishing. [Link](https://www.brookings.edu/books/art-for-arts-sake-the-impact-of-arts-education/)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: There is little rigorous evidence that arts education improves achievement in other school subjects. A few specific links hold up better, such as music with phonological skills and classroom drama with verbal skills. The authors conclude the arts are justified by what they teach in themselves.
- Limits: An OECD book. Its conclusions are summarised from prior knowledge; the publisher page read on the check date shows no findings. Its search predates the arts trials by Bowen and Kisida (`bowen-2023`).
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: music.

### `bowen-2014`

Bowen, D. H., Greene, J. P., & Kisida, B. (2014). Learning to think critically: A visual art experiment. Educational Researcher. [Link](https://www.artsedsearch.org/study/learning-to-think-critically-a-visual-art-experiment/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 8 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: 3,811 students in grades 3-12 were assigned by lottery to a guided art museum visit. Visitors used more critical-thinking strategies when writing about an unfamiliar painting, with the largest gains among younger and disadvantaged students.
- Limits: Read from a research-database summary. Thinking about art only; no transfer was tested. The visit came with classroom lessons, so the active ingredient is unclear.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `bowen-2023`

Bowen, D. H., & Kisida, B. (2023). Investigating the causal effects of arts education. Journal of Policy Analysis and Management. [Link](https://econpapers.repec.org/RePEc:wly:jpamgt:v:42:y:2023:i:3:p:624-647)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 5 y to 14 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In 42 Houston elementary and middle schools randomly assigned more arts learning through community partnerships, students had fewer disciplinary infractions, better writing achievement and more emotional empathy. Elementary students also became more engaged in school and had higher college aspirations.
- Limits: Read from an abstract page with no effect sizes. School-wide arts programs, not home activity.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).
- Also informs: music.

### `goldstein-2018`

Goldstein, T. R., & Lerner, M. D. (2018). Dramatic pretend play games uniquely improve emotional control in young children. Developmental Science. [Link](https://www.artsedsearch.org/study/dramatic-pretend-play-games-uniquely-improve-emotional-control-in-young-children/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 4 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Low-income children aged 4-6 were randomly assigned to eight weeks of dramatic pretend play games, block play or storytime. Only the drama group improved, and only on emotional self-control; there was no effect on social skills, empathy or theory of mind.
- Limits: Read from a research-database summary. One sample, no long-term follow-up.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `brown-2010`

Brown, E. D., Benedett, B., & Armistead, M. E. (2010). Arts enrichment and school readiness for children at risk. Early Childhood Research Quarterly. [Link](https://settlementmusic.org/app/uploads/2018/10/ArtsEnrichmentandSchoolReadiness.pdf)

- Design: quasi-experiment. Ages studied: 3 y to 5 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: In a Head Start preschool with daily music, dance and visual-arts classes, two years of attendance were linked to higher achievement than one, and after one year children had larger receptive vocabularies than children at a comparison preschool.
- Limits: Not randomised. The program differed from the comparison in more than the arts.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: music.

### `brown-sax-2013`

Brown, E. D., & Sax, K. L. (2013). Arts enrichment and preschool emotions for low-income children at risk. Early Childhood Research Quarterly. [Link](https://www.artsedsearch.org/study/arts-enrichment-and-preschool-emotions-for-low-income-children-at-risk)

- Design: quasi-experiment. Ages studied: 3 y to 5 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: 205 Head Start children (174 in the arts program, 31 comparison) were followed for a year. Arts-program children showed more positive emotion and more growth in emotion regulation.
- Limits: Read from a research-database summary. Two buildings compared, with a small comparison group.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `brown-2017`

Brown, E. D., Garnett, M. L., Anderson, K. E., & Laurenceau, J.-P. (2017). Can the arts get under the skin? Arts and cortisol for economically disadvantaged children. Child Development. [Link](https://digitalcommons.wcupa.edu/psych_facpub/5)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 3 y to 5 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: 310 Head Start children aged 3-5 had lower cortisol after music, dance and visual-arts classes than after ordinary homeroom classes in the middle and at the end of the year, but not at the start.
- Limits: Cortisol is a stress marker, not a behaviour. Disadvantaged sample.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: music, social-emotional.

### `fan-2023`

Fan, J. E., Bainbridge, W. A., Chamberlain, R., & Wammes, J. D. (2023). Drawing as a versatile cognitive tool. Nature Reviews Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11377027/)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 75 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Drawing combines perception, memory and social inference; it is used both to record what one sees and to communicate and learn. Evidence on when drawing improves learning is mixed.
- Limits: A broad review, mostly of adults.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: science.

### `butler-1995`

Butler, S., Gross, J., & Hayne, H. (1995). The effect of drawing on memory performance in young children. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://core.ac.uk/download/46951793.pdf)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 5 y to 6 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Five- and six-year-olds asked to draw while describing a recent outing reported more correct information than children who only told about it.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. A single lab study.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: writing.

### `scott-2004`

Scott, G., Leritz, L. E., & Mumford, M. D. (2004). The effectiveness of creativity training: A quantitative review. Creativity Research Journal. [Link](https://scispace.com/papers/the-effectiveness-of-creativity-training-a-quantitative-gui0bxeg94)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 6 y to 75 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 70 studies, well-designed creativity training produced gains that generalised across measures, settings and groups. Programs that taught cognitive skills, such as finding problems and combining ideas, worked best.
- Limits: Read from an aggregator's copy of the abstract. Few studies involved children under 6.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).
- Also informs: cross-cutting.

### `greene-2017`

Greene, J. P., Erickson, H. H., Watson, A. R., & Beck, M. I. (2017). The play's the thing: Experimentally examining the social and cognitive effects of school field trips to live theater performances. EDRE Working Paper. [Link](https://scholarworks.uark.edu/edrepub/7)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 7 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In five lottery experiments over two years, students who saw live theatre gained in tolerance, social perspective taking, and knowledge of the plot and vocabulary; students who saw the film version did not.
- Limits: A working paper. Ages are not given in the abstract; school-age students.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `catterall-2012`

Catterall, J. S., Dumais, S. A., & Hampden-Thompson, G. (2012). The arts and achievement in at-risk youth: Findings from four longitudinal studies. National Endowment for the Arts Research Report 55. [Link](https://arts.gov/sites/default/files/Arts-At-Risk-Youth.pdf)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 5 y to 26 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: In four national US datasets, low-income students with high arts involvement had better school results than low-income students with little arts involvement, for example 8th-grade science scores of 79 against 72 out of 100.
- Limits: Correlational. The report says causation is not established.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `mages-2008`

Mages, W. K. (2008). Does creative drama promote language development in early childhood? A review of the methods and measures employed in the empirical literature. Review of Educational Research. [Link](https://education-eng.macam.ac.il/article/595)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 8 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Reviewed the studies of creative drama and young children's language and found methodological problems that undermine their validity, reliability and credibility.
- Limits: Read from a journal-listing summary. A review of methods, so it gives no effect estimate.

### `podlozny-2000`

Podlozny, A. (2000). Strengthening verbal skills through the use of classroom drama: A clear link. Journal of Aesthetic Education. [Link](https://www.artsedsearch.org/study/strengthening-verbal-skills-through-the-use-of-classroom-drama-a-clear-link/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 4 y to 12 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Seven meta-analyses of 80 studies linked classroom drama with six of seven verbal outcomes, including story recall and oral language. Enacting a story with a set plot gave larger effects than free improvisation.

### `rose-2006`

Rose, S. E., Jolley, R. P., & Burkitt, E. (2006). A review of children's, teachers' and parents' influences on children's drawing experience. International Journal of Art and Design Education. [Link](https://oro.open.ac.uk/16080)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 5 y to 14 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Reviewed how children, teachers and parents shape drawing experience and reported preliminary survey data from 270 children aged 5-14 on a decline in drawing with age.

- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `lobo-2006`

Lobo, Y. B., & Winsler, A. (2006). The effects of a creative dance and movement program on the social competence of Head Start preschoolers. Social Development. [Link](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/WWC/Study/90051)

### `root-bernstein-2008`

Root-Bernstein, R., et al. (2008). Arts foster scientific success: Avocations of Nobel, National Academy, Royal Society, and Sigma Xi members. Journal of Psychology of Science and Technology. [Link](https://www.arts.gov/sites/default/files/Root-Bernstein-PPT.pdf)
