## Music

### `sala-2020`

Sala, G., & Gobet, F. (2020). Cognitive and academic benefits of music training with children: A multilevel meta-analysis. Memory & Cognition. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32728850/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 16 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across 54 studies, music training showed a small overall effect on cognitive and academic outcomes that fell to about zero in studies with random assignment and active control groups.
- Limits: It addresses transfer to other skills, not the value of learning music.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `schellenberg-2004`

Schellenberg, E. G. (2004). Music lessons enhance IQ. Psychological Science. [Link](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/journals/psychological-science/j.0956-7976.2004.00711.x/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 6 y to 7 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: 144 children were randomly assigned to a year of keyboard lessons, voice lessons, drama lessons or no lessons. The two music groups gained more in full-scale IQ than the controls, an effect the author calls relatively small. The drama group gained in social behaviour instead.
- Limits: One trial with 6-year-olds. Later meta-analyses with active controls find no reliable IQ effect (`sala-2020`).
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `kirschner-2010`

Kirschner, S., & Tomasello, M. (2010). Joint music making promotes prosocial behavior in 4-year-old children. Evolution and Human Behavior. [Link](https://www.eva.mpg.de/documents/Elsevier/Kirschner_Joint_EvolHumBeh_2010_1552719.pdf)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 4 y to 4 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: 96 children aged 4 to 5 (48 pairs) played a game together with or without singing and drumming. Afterwards the music pairs helped and cooperated with each other more often than the matched non-music pairs.
- Limits: One lab session with an immediate test. The authors could not separate music from joint rhythmic activity in general. Durable effects are untested.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `woodruff-2014`

Woodruff Carr, K., White-Schwoch, T., Tierney, A. T., Strait, D. L., & Kraus, N. (2014). Beat synchronization predicts neural speech encoding and reading readiness in preschoolers. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25246562/)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 3 y to 4 y 11 mo. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Preschoolers who could tap in time to a beat showed more faithful neural encoding of the rhythm of speech and higher early language scores than those who could not.
- Limits: Correlational. It does not show that beat training improves language.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: reading.

### `roman-caballero-2022`

Román-Caballero, R., Vadillo, M. A., Trainor, L. J., & Lupiáñez, J. (2022). Please don't stop the music: A meta-analysis of the cognitive and academic benefits of instrumental musical training in childhood and adolescence. Educational Research Review. [Link](https://digibug.ugr.es/handle/10481/72632)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Reanalysing the trial literature with different inclusion choices, the authors found a small positive effect of instrumental training on cognitive and academic outcomes, and argued that previous null conclusions were driven by analytic choices.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the repository page blocked automated reading. It directly disputes `sala-2020`, so the question is contested, not settled.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `bigand-tillmann-2022`

Bigand, E., & Tillmann, B. (2022). Near and far transfer: Is music special? Memory & Cognition. [Link](https://hal.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-03384381)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Reanalysed the Sala and Gobet data and argued that, with different study selection, music training shows a small positive effect on cognitive skills.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page blocked automated reading. A reply to `sala-2020`, not new data.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `gordon-2015`

Gordon, R. L., Fehd, H. M., & McCandliss, B. D. (2015). Does music training enhance literacy skills? A meta-analysis. Frontiers in Psychology. [Link](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4664655/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 4 y to 13 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 13 studies, music training produced a small gain in phonological awareness and no reliable gain in reading fluency.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date. Few studies, mixed designs.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: reading.

### `neves-2022`

Neves, L., Correia, A. I., Castro, S. L., Martins, D., & Lima, C. F. (2022). Does music training enhance auditory and linguistic processing? A systematic review and meta-analysis of behavioral and brain evidence. Neuroscience & Biobehavioral Reviews. [Link](https://www.pubmed.gov/35843347/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 62 longitudinal studies with 3,928 participants, music training had a small positive effect on auditory and linguistic measures, whatever the assignment method, training type or control group.
- Limits: One test suggested publication bias and another did not; the authors say further studies are needed to rule it out. Reading itself is not the main outcome.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: reading.

### `costa-giomi-1999`

Costa-Giomi, E. (1999). The effects of three years of piano instruction on children's cognitive development. Journal of Research in Music Education. [Link](https://www.sciencegate.app/document/10.2307/3345779)

- Design: quasi-experiment. Ages studied: 9 y to 12 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: 117 children in grades 4-6, 63 given individual piano lessons and 54 not, did not differ at the start. The piano group had higher spatial scores after one and two years, but the groups no longer differed on any ability after three years. There was no effect on verbal or quantitative skills.
- Limits: Read from an aggregator's copy of the abstract. Older children than the 4-6 band.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `moreno-2011`

Moreno, S., Bialystok, E., Barac, R., Schellenberg, E. G., Cepeda, N. J., & Chau, T. (2011). Short-term music training enhances verbal intelligence and executive function. Psychological Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3449320)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 4 y to 6 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Children aged 4-6 given 20 days of computer-based music listening training improved more on verbal intelligence than children given visual-art training.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date. Short, small and not well replicated.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `mehr-2013`

Mehr, S. A., Schachner, A., Katz, R. C., & Spelke, E. S. (2013). Two randomized trials provide no consistent evidence for nonmusical cognitive benefits of brief preschool music enrichment. PLoS ONE. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3859544)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 4 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In two randomized trials with 4-year-olds, six weeks of parent-and-child music classes did not consistently improve spatial, linguistic or numerical skills compared with visual-arts classes or no classes.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date. Brief classes only.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `dege-2011`

Degé, F., & Schwarzer, G. (2011). The effect of a music program on phonological awareness in preschoolers. Frontiers in Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3121007)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 5 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: 41 preschoolers aged 5-6 were randomly assigned to a music program, a phonological-skills program or a sports program. The music and phonological groups both improved phonological awareness for large units such as words and syllables; the sports group did not. No group improved more on single sounds.
- Limits: Small sample, one study. Home practice was not measured.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: reading.

### `linnavalli-2018`

Linnavalli, T., Putkinen, V., Lipsanen, J., Huotilainen, M., & Tervaniemi, M. (2018). Music playschool enhances children's linguistic skills. Scientific Reports. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5993803)

- Design: quasi-experiment. Ages studied: 5 y to 7 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Over about two years, Finnish kindergarteners in weekly music playschool improved more in phonemic awareness and vocabulary than children in dance lessons or neither.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date. Groups were not randomly assigned.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: reading.

### `williams-2015`

Williams, K. E., Barrett, M. S., Welch, G. F., Abad, V., & Broughton, M. (2015). Associations between early shared music activities in the home and later child outcomes: Findings from the Longitudinal Study of Australian Children. Early Childhood Research Quarterly. [Link](https://discovery-pp.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/1496686)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 2 y to 4 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 3,031 Australian children, more frequent shared music at home at ages 2-3 had small associations at 4-5 with vocabulary, numeracy, attention and emotion regulation, and prosocial skills. With shared book reading controlled, small associations remained for prosocial skills, attention regulation and numeracy.
- Limits: Correlational and small. The authors say only that home music may have a role.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `rabinowitch-2013`

Rabinowitch, T.-C., Cross, I., & Burnard, P. (2013). Long-term musical group interaction has a positive influence on empathy in children. Psychology of Music. [Link](https://www.repository.cam.ac.uk/handle/1810/294755)

- Design: quasi-experiment. Ages studied: 8 y to 11 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Children who took part in a school year of musical group games scored higher on emotional empathy at the end than at the start, and higher than control children.
- Limits: Small. Ages from prior knowledge; the abstract read does not give the sample.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `guhn-2020`

Guhn, M., Emerson, S. D., & Gouzouasis, P. (2020). A population-level analysis of associations between school music participation and academic achievement. Journal of Educational Psychology. [Link](https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2019/06/music-students-score-better)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 6 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In more than 112,000 British Columbia students, those who took school music in grades 10-12 had higher exam scores in math, science and English, more so for instrumental music, after controlling for background and grade 7 scores.
- Limits: Read from a press release. Associations only: students choose music, and the `mosing-2016` and `corrigall-2013` findings suggest who chooses it explains much of this.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `mcpherson-2005`

McPherson, G. E. (2005). From child to musician: Skill development during the beginning stages of learning an instrument. Psychology of Music. [Link](https://findanexpert.unimelb.edu.au/scholarlywork/1231882-from-child-to-musician--skill-development-during-the-beginning-stages-of-learning-an-instrument)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 7 y to 9 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Following about 150 children who started band instruments at 7-9 over three years, the amount of practice mattered, but how they practised, using mental strategies such as working out problem passages, predicted progress more.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Older beginners than 4-6.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `kraus-2014`

Kraus, N., Slater, J., Thompson, E. C., Hornickel, J., Strait, D. L., Nicol, T., & White-Schwoch, T. (2014). Music enrichment programs improve the neural encoding of speech in at-risk children. Journal of Neuroscience. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6608462)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 6 y to 9 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: In a community music program, children randomly assigned to two years of training showed sharper neural encoding of speech sounds; one year was not enough.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge. A published comment disputed the analysis. A brain measure, not a school or skill outcome.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `hyde-2009`

Hyde, K. L., Lerch, J., Norton, A., Forgeard, M., Winner, E., Evans, A. C., & Schlaug, G. (2009). Musical training shapes structural brain development. Journal of Neuroscience. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19279238/)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 5 y to 7 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: After 15 months of keyboard lessons in early childhood, children showed structural brain changes in motor and auditory areas that correlated with gains in musically relevant motor and auditory skills.
- Limits: Small and not randomised. It shows the brain adapts to the trained skill, not transfer to other skills.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `demorest-2015`

Demorest, S. M., & Pfordresher, P. Q. (2015). Singing accuracy development from K-adult: A comparative study. Music Perception. [Link](https://news.northwestern.edu/stories/2015/02/cant-sing-keep-at-it)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 5 y to 22 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Singing in tune improved from kindergarten to late elementary school. College students, most of whom had stopped singing, performed at the kindergarten level on two of three tasks.
- Limits: Read from a university news story. Cross-sectional: the adult decline is consistent with, but does not prove, 'use it or lose it'.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `ilari-2016`

Ilari, B., Keller, P., Damasio, H., & Habibi, A. (2016). The development of musical skills of underprivileged children over the course of 1 year: A study in the context of an El Sistema-inspired program. Frontiers in Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4735430)

- Design: quasi-experiment. Ages studied: 6 y to 7 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Over one year, 23 children aged 6-7 in an El Sistema-inspired program developed pitch skills faster than rhythm skills, while 27 comparison children declined in singing and pitch discrimination.
- Limits: Small, one program, self-selected group.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `mosing-2016`

Mosing, M. A., Madison, G., Pedersen, N. L., & Ullén, F. (2016). Investigating cognitive transfer within the framework of music practice: Genetic pleiotropy rather than causality. Developmental Science. [Link](https://zendy.io/title/10.1111/desc.12306)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 18 y to 75 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In about 10,000 Swedish twins, people who had practised music more had higher IQ, but within identical twin pairs the twin who practised more did not have higher IQ, pointing to shared genes and family rather than practice as the cause.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Adults recalling practice.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `corrigall-2013`

Corrigall, K. A., Schellenberg, E. G., & Misura, N. M. (2013). Music training, cognition, and personality. Frontiers in Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3639373)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 10 y to 12 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Among 10- to 12-year-olds, the link between music lessons and cognitive scores was largely accounted for by parents' education and the child's personality, especially openness to experience.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Correlational.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

## Movement and sports

### `who-2019`

World Health Organization. (2019). Guidelines on physical activity, sedentary behaviour and sleep for children under 5 years of age. [Link](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/9789241550536)

- Design: guideline. Ages studied: 0 mo to 4 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Children aged 3-4 should get at least 180 minutes of physical activity a day, including at least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity, no more than one hour of sedentary screen time, and 10-13 hours of good-quality sleep.
- Limits: WHO rates the underlying evidence as low or very low quality. The guideline stops at age 4.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `us-pag-2018`

U.S. Department of Health and Human Services. (2018). Physical activity guidelines for Americans (2nd ed.). [Link](https://health.gov/sites/default/files/2019-10/PAG_ExecutiveSummary.pdf)

- Design: guideline. Ages studied: 3 y to 17 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Children aged 3-5 should be physically active throughout the day. From age 6, children need at least 60 minutes a day of moderate-to-vigorous activity, including muscle- and bone-strengthening activity.
- Limits: A guideline, with the preschool recommendation resting on thinner evidence than the school-age one.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `logan-2012`

Logan, S. W., Robinson, L. E., Wilson, A. E., & Lucas, W. A. (2012). Getting the fundamentals of movement: A meta-analysis of the effectiveness of motor skill interventions in children. Child: Care, Health and Development. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21880055/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 10 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Planned motor skill instruction improved children's fundamental movement skills (running, jumping, throwing, catching, kicking). Comparison groups who only had free play did not improve.
- Limits: Eleven studies, many with children who had delays or were from low-income families, and short-term outcomes.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `stodden-2008`

Stodden, D. F., Goodway, J. D., Langendorfer, S. J., Roberton, M. A., Rudisill, M. E., Garcia, C., & Garcia, L. E. (2008). A developmental perspective on the role of motor skill competence in physical activity: An emergent relationship. Quest. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1080/00336297.2008.10483582)

- Design: theory. Ages studied: 2 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Proposes that motor skill competence in early childhood drives later physical activity, perceived competence and fitness, and that the link strengthens with age. Children who lack the basic skills drop out of active play and sport.
- Limits: A conceptual model. See robinson-2015 for the supporting evidence.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `robinson-2015`

Robinson, L. E., Stodden, D. F., Barnett, L. M., Lopes, V. P., Logan, S. W., Rodrigues, L. P., & D'Hondt, E. (2015). Motor competence and its effect on positive developmental trajectories of health. Sports Medicine. [Link](https://link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s40279-015-0351-6)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 2 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Reviews evidence that motor competence is positively related to physical activity, fitness and perceived competence, and inversely related to weight status, across childhood.
- Limits: Mostly correlational and cross-sectional studies.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `aap-sports-2019`

Logan, K., Cuff, S., & Council on Sports Medicine and Fitness. (2019). Organized sports for children, preadolescents, and adolescents. Pediatrics. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31110166/)

- Design: guideline. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Organized sport has physical, social and psychological benefits when it stays fun and matches the child's development. Before children are developmentally ready, free play and basic skills matter more than competition. Fun is the main reason children keep playing.
- Limits: A clinical report based on expert review. The report places readiness for organized sport at about age 6 for most children; that figure is recalled from memory and should be confirmed in the report.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `aap-specialization-2016`

Brenner, J. S., & Council on Sports Medicine and Fitness. (2016). Sports specialization and intensive training in young athletes. Pediatrics. [Link](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/138/3/e20162148/52612/Sports-Specialization-and-Intensive-Training-in)

- Design: guideline. Ages studied: 5 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Playing several sports and delaying single-sport specialization until late adolescence (about 15-16 for most sports) is associated with fewer injuries and less stress and burnout, and does not reduce the chance of athletic success.
- Limits: Based largely on observational studies of older athletes.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `brussoni-2015`

Brussoni, M., Gibbons, R., Gray, C., Ishikawa, T., Sandseter, E. B. H., Bienenstock, A., et al. (2015). What is the relationship between risky outdoor play and health in children? A systematic review. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4483710)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 12 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 21 papers, risky outdoor play (heights, speed, rough-and-tumble, playing out of sight) was associated with more physical activity and better social health. Play at height was not associated with more or worse fractures.
- Limits: Evidence quality rated low to moderate, mostly observational.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: nature, social-emotional.

### `brenner-2009`

Brenner, R. A., Taneja, G. S., Haynie, D. L., Trumble, A. C., Qian, C., Klinger, R. M., & Klebanoff, M. A. (2009). Association between swimming lessons and drowning in childhood: A case-control study. Archives of Pediatrics & Adolescent Medicine. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19255386)

- Design: case-control. Ages studied: 12 mo to 4 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Formal swimming lessons were associated with an 88% lower risk of drowning in children aged 1-4 (odds ratio 0.12, 95% confidence interval 0.01 to 0.97).
- Limits: Case-control design with a very wide confidence interval. Lessons do not make a child drown-proof.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `aap-drowning-2019`

Denny, S. A., Quan, L., Gilchrist, J., McCallin, T., Shenoi, R., Yusuf, S., et al. (2019). Prevention of drowning. Pediatrics. [Link](https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/143/5/e20190850/37134/Prevention-of-Drowning)

- Design: guideline. Ages studied: 12 mo to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Recommends swim lessons for most children from about age 1 as one layer of protection alongside close supervision, pool barriers and life jackets.
- Limits: Newer AAP drowning statements (2021 and 2026) appeared in search results and were not reviewed.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `wick-2017`

Wick, K., Leeger-Aschmann, C. S., Monn, N. D., Radtke, T., Ott, L. V., Rebholz, C. E., et al. (2017). Interventions to promote fundamental movement skills in childcare and kindergarten: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Sports Medicine. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5603621)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 2 y to 7 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Structured movement-skill programs in childcare and kindergarten improved children's fundamental movement skills compared with usual activity.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `eime-2013`

Eime, R. M., Young, J. A., Harvey, J. T., Charity, M. J., & Payne, W. R. (2013). A systematic review of the psychological and social benefits of participation in sport for children and adolescents. International Journal of Behavioral Nutrition and Physical Activity. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3751802)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 6 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: A review of 30 studies found sport participation associated with higher self-esteem, better social interaction and fewer depressive symptoms, with team sport associated with better outcomes than individual activities.
- Limits: 21 of the 30 studies were cross-sectional, so the direction of cause is unclear.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `visek-2015`

Visek, A. J., Achrati, S. M., Mannix, H., McDonnell, K., Harris, B. S., & DiPietro, L. (2015). The fun integration theory: Toward sustaining children and adolescents sport participation. Journal of Physical Activity and Health. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4201634)

- Design: observational. Ages studied: 8 y to 19 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Concept mapping with 142 youth soccer players, 37 coaches and 57 parents produced 81 things that make sport fun, grouped into 11 dimensions such as trying hard, positive coaching and learning and improving.
- Limits: Older children. That winning ranked low is from prior knowledge, not the abstract read.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `carson-2017`

Carson, V., Lee, E.-Y., Hewitt, L., Jennings, C., Hunter, S., Kuzik, N., et al. (2017). Systematic review of the relationships between physical activity and health indicators in the early years (0-4 years). BMC Public Health. [Link](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5753397/)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 0 mo to 4 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Physical activity in children up to age 4 was favourably associated with motor development, fitness, bone health and cardiometabolic health, with weaker evidence for cognitive development.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Basis of guideline `who-2019`.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `sandseter-2011`

Sandseter, E. B. H., & Kennair, L. E. O. (2011). Children's risky play from an evolutionary perspective: The anti-phobic effects of thrilling experiences. Evolutionary Psychology. [Link](https://www.pubmed.gov/22947972/)

- Design: theory. Ages studied: 3 y to 12 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Proposed that thrilling play with heights, speed and rough-and-tumble exposes children to fears in manageable doses and may protect against later anxiety.
- Limits: A theoretical argument, not a test.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `jayanthi-2015`

Jayanthi, N. A., LaBella, C. R., Fischer, D., Pasulka, J., & Dugas, L. R. (2015). Sports-specialized intensive training and the risk of injury in young athletes: A clinical case-control study. American Journal of Sports Medicine. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/25646361/)

- Design: case-control. Ages studied: 7 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Among 1,190 athletes aged 7-18, highly specialised athletes, and those training more hours a week than their age in years, had higher odds of serious overuse injuries.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Older children.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

## Social-emotional skills

### `jones-2015`

Jones, D. E., Greenberg, M., & Crowley, M. (2015). Early social-emotional functioning and public health: The relationship between kindergarten social competence and future wellness. American Journal of Public Health. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4605168)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 5 y to 25 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 753 kindergartners, teacher-rated prosocial skill predicted education, employment, crime, substance use and mental health 13-19 years later, controlling for family and child characteristics.
- Limits: Correlational, in a sample weighted toward higher-risk children.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `moffitt-2011`

Moffitt, T. E., Arseneault, L., Belsky, D., Dickson, N., Hancox, R. J., Harrington, H., et al. (2011). A gradient of childhood self-control predicts health, wealth, and public safety. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3041102)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 3 y to 32 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In about 1,000 children followed to age 32, childhood self-control predicted adult health, finances and criminal offending along a gradient, controlling for intelligence and social class.
- Limits: Observational. It does not show that training self-control changes those outcomes.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `watts-2018`

Watts, T. W., Duncan, G. J., & Quan, H. (2018). Revisiting the marshmallow test: A conceptual replication investigating links between early delay of gratification and later outcomes. Psychological Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7197218)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y 6 mo to 15 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In a larger and more diverse sample, the link between delay of gratification at 54 months and achievement at 15 was half the size originally reported, and shrank by about two thirds once family background and early cognitive ability were controlled.
- Limits: A replication of a correlation. It cautions against treating one self-control task as a lever.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `diamond-2011`

Diamond, A., & Lee, K. (2011). Interventions shown to aid executive function development in children 4 to 12 years old. Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3159917/)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 4 y to 12 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Computerized training, aerobic exercise, martial arts, mindfulness and some school curricula improved executive function. Children with the weakest executive function gained most, gains needed the challenge to keep rising, and transfer was narrow.
- Limits: A narrative review. Several of the headline programs have had mixed results since.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: movement.

### `leonard-2021`

Leonard, J. A., Martinez, D. N., Dashineau, S. C., Park, A. T., & Mackey, A. P. (2021). Children persist less when adults take over. Child Development. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1111/cdev.13492)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 4 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Parents who took over more during a hard puzzle had 4-5-year-olds rated as less persistent. In an experiment, children persisted less on a later task after an adult took over than after an adult taught them or did nothing.
- Limits: Short lab tasks and immediate effects.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: cross-cutting.

### `gunderson-2013`

Gunderson, E. A., Gripshover, S. J., Romero, C., Dweck, C. S., Goldin-Meadow, S., & Levine, S. C. (2013). Parent praise to 1- to 3-year-olds predicts children's motivational frameworks 5 years later. Child Development. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3655123)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 14 mo to 8 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: The share of parents' praise that was about effort and strategy when children were 14-38 months old predicted the children's belief, at age 7-8, that ability can grow.
- Limits: 53 families, correlational. See sisk-2018 for how small mindset effects on achievement are.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `sisk-2018`

Sisk, V. F., Burgoyne, A. P., Sun, J., Butler, J. L., & Macnamara, B. N. (2018). To what extent and under which circumstances are growth mind-sets important to academic achievement? Two meta-analyses. Psychological Science. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/29505339/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 5 y to 25 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Mindset is only weakly related to academic achievement, and mindset interventions have very small average effects, somewhat larger for academically at-risk students.
- Limits: School-age to adult samples.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `vasquez-2016`

Vasquez, A. C., Patall, E. A., Fong, C. J., Corrigan, A. S., & Pine, L. (2016). Parent autonomy support, academic achievement, and psychosocial functioning: A meta-analysis of research. Educational Psychology Review. [Link](https://link.springer.com/doi/10.1007/s10648-015-9329-z)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Parents' support for their children's autonomy was related to better achievement, motivation and psychological health.
- Limits: A meta-analysis of correlations, mostly in school-age children.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: practical-life.

### `denham-2003`

Denham, S. A., Blair, K. A., DeMulder, E., Levitas, J., Sawyer, K., Auerbach-Major, S., & Queenan, P. (2003). Preschool emotional competence: Pathway to social competence? Child Development. [Link](https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-8624.00533)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 3 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 143 preschoolers, emotional expressiveness, emotion regulation and emotion knowledge at ages 3-4 predicted social competence in kindergarten.
- Limits: Correlational.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `obradovic-2021`

Obradović, J., Sulik, M. J., & Shaffer, A. (2021). Learning to let go: Parental over-engagement predicts poorer self-regulation in kindergartners. Journal of Family Psychology. [Link](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2021/03/study-reveals-impact-much-parental-involvement)

- Design: observational. Ages studied: 5 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In videotaped play with about 100 kindergartners, parents who kept directing, teaching or correcting while the child was already engaged had children with poorer self-regulation in tasks and in teacher reports.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Correlational.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `perry-2018`

Perry, N. B., Dollar, J. M., Calkins, S. D., Keane, S. P., & Shanahan, L. (2018). Childhood self-regulation as a mechanism through which early overcontrolling parenting is associated with adjustment in preadolescence. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6062452)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 2 y to 10 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 422 children assessed at 2, 5 and 10, overcontrolling parenting at age 2 was associated with poorer emotion and behaviour regulation at 5, and better regulation at 5 with fewer emotional problems and better school and social outcomes at 10.
- Limits: Read from a press release. Correlational.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `rapee-2005`

Rapee, R. M., Kennedy, S., Ingram, M., Edwards, S., & Sweeney, L. (2005). Prevention and early intervention of anxiety disorders in inhibited preschool children. Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15982146/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 3 y 6 mo to 4 y 6 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In 146 very shy preschoolers, six parent group sessions on reducing overprotection and encouraging gradual exposure led to fewer anxiety diagnoses a year later than no intervention.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Children selected for high inhibition.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `lebowitz-2020`

Lebowitz, E. R., Marin, C., Martino, A., Shimshoni, Y., & Silverman, W. K. (2020). Parent-based treatment as efficacious as cognitive-behavioral therapy for childhood anxiety: A randomized noninferiority study of Supportive Parenting for Anxious Childhood Emotions. Journal of the American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6732048)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 7 y to 14 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In 124 children aged 7-14 with an anxiety disorder, 12 weekly sessions of a parent-only program that taught parents to reduce accommodation of the child's anxiety and express confidence in the child reduced anxiety as much as CBT delivered to the child.
- Limits: Read from an NIH summary; published online in 2019. Clinical sample, older children.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `mueller-dweck-1998`

Mueller, C. M., & Dweck, C. S. (1998). Praise for intelligence can undermine children's motivation and performance. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. [Link](https://www.columbia.edu/cu/psychology/courses/3615/Readings/Mueller_Dweck.pdf)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 10 y to 11 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In six studies, starting with 128 fifth graders, children praised for intelligence after a success persisted less, enjoyed the task less and performed worse after a later failure than children praised for effort.
- Limits: Older children. See `li-bates-2019` for failed replications.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `li-bates-2019`

Li, Y., & Bates, T. C. (2019). You can't change your basic ability, but you work at things, and that's how we get hard things done: Testing the role of growth mindset on response to setbacks, educational attainment, and cognitive ability. Journal of Experimental Psychology: General. [Link](https://westminsterresearch.westminster.ac.uk/item/v62v1/you-can-t-change-your-basic-ability-but-you-work-at-things-and-that-s-how-we-get-hard-things-done-testing-the-role-of-growth-mindset-on-response-to-setbacks-educational-attainment-and-cognitive)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 9 y to 13 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In three studies with more than 600 children aged 9-13 in China and the UK, a growth-mindset manipulation did not improve resilience after failure, and mindset was not related to grades.
- Limits: Read from a university news release.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `brummelman-2014`

Brummelman, E., Thomaes, S., Orobio de Castro, B., Overbeek, G., & Bushman, B. J. (2014). "That's not just beautiful - that's incredibly beautiful!": The adverse impact of inflated praise on children with low self-esteem. Psychological Science. [Link](https://dare.uva.nl/id/a865c3f8-ca77-486a-a152-0fabd59f91f7)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 8 y to 12 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Adults gave inflated praise about twice as often to children with low self-esteem. In an experiment with 240 children, children with low self-esteem who were told a drawing was 'incredibly beautiful' then chose easier drawings to copy; children with high self-esteem chose harder ones.
- Limits: Read from a press release. Older children.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).
- Also informs: art.

### `havighurst-2010`

Havighurst, S. S., Wilson, K. R., Harley, A. E., Prior, M. R., & Kehoe, C. (2010). Tuning in to Kids: Improving emotion socialization practices in parents of preschool children - findings from a community trial. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20735794/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 4 y to 5 y 6 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Parents of preschoolers randomised to a six-session emotion-coaching program became less dismissive and more coaching of emotions, and their children's behaviour problems fell more than in the control group.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Parent and teacher reports.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `leonard-2017`

Leonard, J. A., Lee, Y., & Schulz, L. E. (2017). Infants make more attempts to achieve a goal when they see adults persist. Science. [Link](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/113043)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 13 mo to 18 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Fifteen-month-olds who watched an adult try hard and succeed at two tasks tried harder on a new toy than infants who watched the adult succeed easily.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Infants, one lab session.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `gray-2023`

Gray, P., Lancy, D. F., & Bjorklund, D. F. (2023). Decline in independent activity as a cause of decline in children's mental well-being: Summary of the evidence. Journal of Pediatrics. [Link](https://www.sciencedaily.com/releases/2023/03/230309101330.htm)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Argues that the decline over decades in children's opportunity to play, roam and act without adult supervision is a cause of rising anxiety and depression.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. An argument from trends and correlations by advocates of the position.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: practical-life.

### `durlak-2011`

Durlak, J. A., Weissberg, R. P., Dymnicki, A. B., Taylor, R. D., & Schellinger, K. B. (2011). The impact of enhancing students' social and emotional learning: A meta-analysis of school-based universal interventions. Child Development. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21291449/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 5 y to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across 213 school programs for about 270,000 students from kindergarten to high school, social and emotional learning programs improved social-emotional skills, attitudes and behaviour, and academic performance by about 11 percentile points.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Later work suggests smaller effects in independent evaluations.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `murano-2020`

Murano, D., Sawyer, J. E., & Lipnevich, A. A. (2020). A meta-analytic review of preschool social and emotional learning interventions. Review of Educational Research. [Link](https://www.researchconnections.org/childcare/resources/38253)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 5 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Preschool social and emotional learning programs improved children's social-emotional competence and reduced problem behaviour.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Classroom programs.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

## Practical life and independence

### `white-2019`

White, E. M., DeBoer, M. D., & Scharf, R. J. (2019). Associations between household chores and childhood self-competency. Journal of Developmental & Behavioral Pediatrics. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30507727/)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 5 y to 9 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: In a national sample of nearly 10,000 children, doing chores more often in kindergarten was associated with higher self-rated competence, prosocial behaviour and math scores in third grade, after controls.
- Limits: Parent-reported chores and correlational. News coverage of a different 2019 longitudinal study reported no link between chores and later self-control; that study was not reviewed.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `tepper-2022`

Tepper, D. L., Howell, T. J., & Bennett, P. C. (2022). Executive functions and household chores: Does engagement in chores predict children's cognition? Australian Occupational Therapy Journal. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC9796572/)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 5 y to 13 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: In parent reports on 207 children aged 5-13, doing self-care and family-care chores was related to better working memory and inhibition. Pet-care chores were not.
- Limits: Cross-sectional parent report. Children with better executive function may simply be given more chores.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `lillard-2017`

Lillard, A. S., Heise, M. J., Richey, E. M., Tong, X., Hart, A., & Bray, P. M. (2017). Montessori preschool elevates and equalizes child outcomes: A longitudinal study. Frontiers in Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5670361)

- Design: quasi-experiment. Ages studied: 3 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Among 141 children whose places were decided by lottery, those in public Montessori preschools did better over three years on academic achievement, social understanding and mastery orientation than those who lost the lottery.
- Limits: Two schools in one city. It tests a whole program, so the result cannot be attributed to practical-life work specifically.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: cross-cutting.

### `randolph-2023`

Randolph, J. J., Bryson, A., Menon, L., Henderson, D. K., Manuel, A. K., Michaels, S., Rosenstein, D. L. W., McPherson, W., O'Grady, R., & Lillard, A. S. (2023). Montessori education's impact on academic and nonacademic outcomes: A systematic review. Campbell Systematic Reviews. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10406168/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 32 studies, Montessori education outperformed traditional education on academic outcomes (g = 0.24) and nonacademic outcomes such as executive function and social skills (g = 0.33).
- Limits: Some outcomes rest on low-quality evidence, publication bias is possible, and it evaluates whole schools, not home practical-life routines.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: cross-cutting.

### `warneken-2008`

Warneken, F., & Tomasello, M. (2008). Extrinsic rewards undermine altruistic tendencies in 20-month-olds. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://scholars.duke.edu/publication/1458228)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 20 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Toddlers who were given a toy as a reward for helping later helped less than toddlers who were praised or given nothing.
- Limits: Toddlers, one lab study.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `bryan-2014`

Bryan, C. J., Master, A., & Walton, G. M. (2014). "Helping" versus "being a helper": Invoking the self to increase helping in young children. Child Development. [Link](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/525469)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 3 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In two experiments with about 150 children aged 3-6, asking children to 'be a helper' led to more helping than asking them 'to help', which did no better than saying nothing.
- Limits: Read from a press release. Immediate lab tasks. See `foster-hanson-2020` for a cost of identity wording.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `foster-hanson-2020`

Foster-Hanson, E., Cimpian, A., Leshin, R. A., & Rhodes, M. (2020). Asking children to "be helpers" can backfire after setbacks. Child Development. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6424657)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 4 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Children aged 4-5 asked to 'be helpers' gave up more readily on helping after a setback, and felt worse about themselves, than children asked 'to help'.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `lillard-2006`

Lillard, A., & Else-Quest, N. (2006). Evaluating Montessori education. Science. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/17008512/)

- Design: quasi-experiment. Ages studied: 5 y to 12 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Children who won a lottery for a public Montessori school did better at 5 on reading, math and executive function than lottery losers, and at 12 on essay writing and social reasoning.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date. One school and high attrition.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: cross-cutting.

### `coppens-2014`

Coppens, A. D., Alcalá, L., Mejía-Arauz, R., & Rogoff, B. (2014). Children's initiative in family household work in Mexico. Human Development. [Link](https://karger.com/hde/article/57/2-3/116/158079/Children-s-Initiative-in-Family-Household-Work-in)

- Design: observational. Ages studied: 9 y to 10 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Almost all mothers in a small Mexican sample said children want to help with household work; children from an Indigenous-heritage community were more often reported to take initiative in broad, complex contributions.
- Limits: 16 families; descriptive. Suggests a cultural pathway in which children join real work rather than being assigned chores.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

## Cooking

### `vanderhorst-2014`

van der Horst, K., Ferrage, A., & Rytz, A. (2014). Involving children in meal preparation. Effects on food intake. Appetite. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/24709485/)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 6 y to 10 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Among 47 children aged 6-10, those who cooked lunch themselves with a parent's help ate 76% more salad, 27% more chicken and 24% more calories than those whose parent cooked alone.
- Limits: One meal, older children, a lab kitchen. The authors note the extra energy intake.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `hersch-2014`

Hersch, D., Perdue, L., Ambroz, T., & Boucher, J. L. (2014). The impact of cooking classes on food-related preferences, attitudes, and behaviors of school-aged children: A systematic review of the evidence, 2003-2014. Preventing Chronic Disease. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4222785)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 5 y to 12 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: A review of 8 studies of cooking programs for children aged 5-12 found they may improve food preferences, attitudes and behaviours.
- Limits: Measures varied too much to identify best practice. Program length, long-term effects and parent involvement are unknown.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `wardle-2003`

Wardle, J., Cooke, L. J., Gibson, E. L., Sapochnik, M., Sheiham, A., & Lawson, M. (2003). Increasing children's acceptance of vegetables; a randomized trial of parent-led exposure. Appetite. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12781165/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 2 y to 6 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: 156 families with children aged 2-6 were randomised. Only children whose parents offered a small taste of a target vegetable every day for 14 days increased their liking and intake of it; nutrition information alone did nothing.
- Limits: One vegetable, short follow-up.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `galloway-2006`

Galloway, A. T., Fiorito, L. M., Francis, L. A., & Birch, L. L. (2006). 'Finish your soup': Counterproductive effects of pressuring children to eat on intake and affect. Appetite. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2604806)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 3 y to 5 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: 27 preschoolers ate significantly more soup, and made far fewer negative comments, when they were not pressured to eat it.
- Limits: Small, one food.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `allirot-2016`

Allirot, X., da Quinta, N., Chokupermal, K., & Urdaneta, E. (2016). Involving children in cooking activities: A potential strategy for directing food choices toward novel foods containing vegetables. Appetite. [Link](https://www.pubmed.gov/27125429/)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 7 y to 11 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: 137 children aged 7-11 who cooked a snack chose more unfamiliar vegetable foods, were more willing to taste them and liked the snack more than children who did not cook, though they did not eat more overall.
- Limits: Older children, one session.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `hammons-fiese-2011`

Hammons, A. J., & Fiese, B. H. (2011). Is frequency of shared family meals related to the nutritional health of children and adolescents? Pediatrics. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3387875)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 2 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 17 studies of 182,836 children and adolescents, three or more family meals a week were associated with lower odds of overweight (OR 0.88) and unhealthy eating (OR 0.80) and higher odds of healthy eating (OR 1.24).
- Limits: Observational: families who eat together differ in other ways.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `decosta-2017`

DeCosta, P., Møller, P., Frøst, M. B., & Olsen, A. (2017). Changing children's eating behaviour: A review of experimental research. Appetite. [Link](https://www.pubmed.gov/28286164/)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 2 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: A review of 120 experimental studies found that controlling feeding strategies appear counterproductive, while hands-on gardening and cooking programs may encourage more vegetable eating.
- Limits: Many short studies.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `chu-2013`

Chu, Y. L., Farmer, A., Fung, C., Kuhle, S., Storey, K. E., & Veugelers, P. J. (2013). Involvement in home meal preparation is associated with food preference and self-efficacy among Canadian children. Public Health Nutrition. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22578854/)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 10 y to 11 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Fifth graders who helped more with meal preparation at home preferred fruit and vegetables more and felt more confident about choosing healthy foods.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page returned no content on the check date. Correlational.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

## Nature and outdoors

### `he-2015`

He, M., Xiang, F., Zeng, Y., Mai, J., Chen, Q., Zhang, J., et al. (2015). Effect of time spent outdoors at school on the development of myopia among children in China: A randomized clinical trial. JAMA. [Link](https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jama/article-abstract/2441261)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 6 y to 9 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In a cluster trial of 1,903 first graders (mean age 6.6) in 12 Guangzhou schools, one extra 40-minute outdoor class each school day cut the 3-year incidence of myopia from 39.5% to 30.4%.
- Limits: School-based in China. The effect on eye length was not significant.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: movement.

### `kuo-2019`

Kuo, M., Barnes, M., & Jordan, C. (2019). Do experiences with nature promote learning? Converging evidence of a cause-and-effect relationship. Frontiers in Psychology. [Link](https://www.frontiersin.org/articles/10.3389/fpsyg.2019.00305/pdf)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Argues that time in nature improves attention, stress, self-discipline and engagement with learning, drawing on experimental and correlational studies.
- Limits: A narrative review by advocates. Many of the underlying studies are small or correlational.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `dankiw-2020`

Dankiw, K. A., Tsiros, M. D., Baldock, K. L., & Kumar, S. (2020). The impacts of unstructured nature play on health in early childhood development: A systematic review. PLoS ONE. [Link](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC7018039/)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 2 y to 12 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Across 16 studies, unstructured play in natural settings was associated with more physical activity and with better cognitive, social and emotional outcomes.
- Limits: Evidence quality rated low, with inconsistent definitions of nature play.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `wu-2018`

Wu, P.-C., Chen, C.-T., Lin, K.-K., Sun, C.-C., Kuo, C.-N., Huang, H.-M., et al. (2018). Myopia prevention and outdoor light intensity in a school-based cluster randomized trial. Ophthalmology. [Link](https://www.pubmed.gov/29371008/)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 6 y to 7 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In 693 first graders in 16 schools, a school outdoor program cut the one-year shift toward myopia (0.35 against 0.47 dioptres) and halved the risk of rapid progression, in children who were and were not already myopic. Strong sunlight did not appear necessary.
- Limits: Taiwanese schools. Some schools withdrew after randomisation.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `xiong-2017`

Xiong, S., Sankaridurg, P., Naduvilath, T., et al. (2017). Time spent in outdoor activities in relation to myopia prevention and control: A meta-analysis and systematic review. Acta Ophthalmologica. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5599950)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across 25 studies, more outdoor time cut the risk of developing myopia by about 46% in trials and 43% in cohort studies, but did not slow progression in eyes already myopic.
- Limits: High heterogeneity between studies.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `ulset-2017`

Ulset, V., Vitaro, F., Brendgen, M., Bekkhus, M., & Borge, A. I. H. (2017). Time spent outdoors during preschool: Links with children's cognitive and behavioral development. Journal of Environmental Psychology. [Link](https://research.childrenandnature.org/?p=2219)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y to 7 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 562 children in 28 Norwegian daycare centres, more outdoor hours at daycare were linked to better working memory and fewer inattention and hyperactivity symptoms from about 4 to 7, after controlling for many confounders.
- Limits: Read from a research summary. Correlational; links weakened at school entry.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `tillmann-2018`

Tillmann, S., Tobin, D., Avison, W., & Gilliland, J. (2018). Mental health benefits of interactions with nature in children and teenagers: A systematic review. Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6161651)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 0 mo to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 35 studies of under-18s, about half of the reported links between nature contact and mental health were positive and almost half were not significant.
- Limits: Mostly cross-sectional; no meta-analysis was possible.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: social-emotional.

### `faber-taylor-2009`

Faber Taylor, A., & Kuo, F. E. (2009). Children with attention deficits concentrate better after walk in the park. Journal of Attention Disorders. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/18725656/)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 7 y to 12 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Seventeen children aged 7-12 with ADHD concentrated better after a 20-minute walk in a park than after walks downtown or in a neighbourhood.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; the page could not be read on the check date. Very small, children with ADHD.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

## Building and engineering

### `verdine-2014`

Verdine, B. N., Golinkoff, R. M., Hirsh-Pasek, K., Newcombe, N. S., Filipowicz, A. T., & Chang, A. (2014). Deconstructing building blocks: Preschoolers' spatial assembly performance relates to early mathematical skills. Child Development. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3962809)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 3 y to 3 y 11 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In about 100 three-year-olds, the ability to copy a block construction from a model was related to early math skill. Children from lower-income families were already behind and heard fewer spatial words.
- Limits: Correlational, in three-year-olds.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: math.

### `uttal-2013`

Uttal, D. H., Meadow, N. G., Tipton, E., Hand, L. L., Alden, A. R., Warren, C., & Newcombe, N. S. (2013). The malleability of spatial skills: A meta-analysis of training studies. Psychological Bulletin. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22663761/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 25 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across 217 training studies, spatial skills improved with practice (average g = 0.47), the gains lasted across delayed tests and transferred to untrained spatial tasks.
- Limits: Most studies were of older children and adults.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `hawes-2022`

Hawes, Z. C. K., Gilligan-Lee, K. A., & Mix, K. S. (2022). Effects of spatial training on mathematics performance: A meta-analysis. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35073120/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Across 29 studies, spatial training improved math performance by roughly a quarter of a standard deviation. Training with physical materials worked better than training without.
- Limits: Effects were larger in older children, and preschool evidence is thin. Moderator details are recalled from memory.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.
- Also informs: math.

### `levine-2012`

Levine, S. C., Ratliff, K. R., Huttenlocher, J., & Cannon, J. (2012). Early puzzle play: A predictor of preschoolers' spatial transformation skill. Developmental Psychology. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3289766)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 2 y 2 mo to 4 y 6 mo. Weight: weak.
- Finding: Children who were seen playing with puzzles between 26 and 46 months had better spatial transformation skill at 54 months, controlling for parent education, income and overall parent talk.
- Limits: 53 families, correlational.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `pruden-2011`

Pruden, S. M., Levine, S. C., & Huttenlocher, J. (2011). Children's spatial thinking: Does talk about the spatial world matter? Developmental Science. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3372906)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 14 mo to 4 y 6 mo. Weight: weak.
- Finding: In 52 children recorded at home from 14 to 46 months, those who heard and produced more spatial words did better on spatial transformation and spatial analogy tasks at 54 months.
- Limits: Correlational. The authors note causal and non-causal explanations both fit, and much of the variation is unexplained.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `jirout-newcombe-2015`

Jirout, J. J., & Newcombe, N. S. (2015). Building blocks for developing spatial skills: Evidence from a large, representative U.S. sample. Psychological Science. [Link](https://www.psychologicalscience.org/observer/blocks-and-puzzles-may-help-children-learn-spatial-skills)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 4 y to 7 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In 847 children aged 4-7, those who played with puzzles, blocks or board games more than six times a week scored higher on a block-design spatial test than those who played less, alongside effects of family income and general ability.
- Limits: Read from a journal-society news article. Correlational.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `fisher-2013`

Fisher, K. R., Hirsh-Pasek, K., Newcombe, N., & Golinkoff, R. M. (2013). Taking shape: Supporting preschoolers' acquisition of geometric knowledge through guided play. Child Development. [Link](https://templeinfantlab.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2019/06/Fisher_et_al-2013-Child_Development.pdf)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 4 y to 5 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: 60 children aged 4 and 5 (mean 56 months) learned about four shapes by guided play, direct instruction or free play. The guided-play group was best at recognising atypical shapes as real triangles, rectangles and so on, and the gain held a week later.
- Limits: Mostly white, upper-middle-class sample; four shapes only.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: math.

### `casey-2008`

Casey, B. M., Andrews, N., Schindler, H., Kersh, J. E., Samper, A., & Copley, J. (2008). The development of spatial skills through interventions involving block building activities. Cognition and Instruction. [Link](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/WWC/Study/78036)

- Design: rct. Ages studied: 5 y to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: The What Works Clearinghouse rated this kindergarten block-building trial as meeting its standards without reservations. Children who built increasingly complex structures, especially within a story, improved on spatial tasks.
- Limits: Results from prior knowledge; the clearinghouse page read did not show effect sizes. Classroom program.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `wai-2009`

Wai, J., Lubinski, D., & Benbow, C. P. (2009). Spatial ability for STEM domains: Aligning over 50 years of cumulative psychological knowledge solidifies its importance. Journal of Educational Psychology. [Link](https://www.Gwern.net/doc/iq/high/smpy/2009-wai.pdf)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 14 y to 33 y 4 mo. Weight: strong.
- Finding: In a US sample of about 400,000 high school students followed for 11 years, spatial ability predicted earning STEM degrees and working in STEM beyond what verbal and math ability predicted.
- Limits: Summary from prior knowledge; not checked on the check date. Adolescent ability; says nothing about training it early.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `wolfgang-2001`

Wolfgang, C. H., Stannard, L. L., & Jones, I. (2001). Block play performance among preschoolers as a predictor of later school achievement in mathematics. Journal of Research in Childhood Education. [Link](https://imaginationplayground.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/04/Block-Play-Performance-Among-Preschoolers.pdf)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 4 y to 18 y. Weight: weak.
- Finding: In 37 children followed from age 4, the complexity of preschool block building did not predict math at grades 3 or 5, but did predict standardised math scores at grade 7 and high-school math course-taking, controlling for IQ, gender and family income.
- Limits: Very small single-preschool sample; the authors say causation was not established.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.
- Also informs: math.

## Second language (optional)

### `kuhl-2003`

Kuhl, P. K., Tsao, F.-M., & Liu, H.-M. (2003). Foreign-language experience in infancy: Effects of short-term exposure and social interaction on phonetic learning. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC166444)

- Design: experiment. Ages studied: 9 mo to 10 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Nine-month-olds learned Mandarin speech-sound contrasts from 12 live sessions with a speaker, but not from the same material on video or audio.
- Limits: Infants and speech-sound learning only.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `hartshorne-2018`

Hartshorne, J. K., Tenenbaum, J. B., & Pinker, S. (2018). A critical period for second language acquisition: Evidence from 2/3 million English speakers. Cognition. [Link](https://dspace.mit.edu/handle/1721.1/126641)

- Design: cross-sectional. Ages studied: 0 mo to 70 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In about 670,000 people, the ability to learn grammar stayed high until about age 17, but reaching a native-like level required starting by about age 10-12.
- Limits: An online English grammar quiz with a self-selected sample.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `byers-2013`

Byers-Heinlein, K., & Lew-Williams, C. (2013). Bilingualism in the early years: What the science says. LEARNing Landscapes. [Link](https://learninglandscapes.ca/index.php/learnland/article/view/632)

- Design: narrative-review. Ages studied: 0 mo to 6 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Children are not confused by hearing two languages. How well each language is learned depends on the amount and quality of exposure to it, and no single family strategy is best.
- Limits: A review written for parents and practitioners.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `lehtonen-2018`

Lehtonen, M., Soveri, A., Laine, A., Jarvenpaa, J., de Bruin, A., & Antfolk, J. (2018). Is bilingualism associated with enhanced executive functioning in adults? A meta-analytic review. Psychological Bulletin. [Link](https://eprints.whiterose.ac.uk/157474/)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 18 y to 80 y. Weight: strong.
- Finding: Across 152 studies of adults, there was no bilingual advantage in executive function once publication bias was corrected.
- Limits: Adults only.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `gunnerud-2020`

Gunnerud, H. L., ten Braak, D., Reikeras, E. K. L., Donolato, E., & Melby-Lervag, M. (2020). Is bilingualism related to a cognitive advantage in children? A systematic review and meta-analysis. Psychological Bulletin. [Link](https://uv.uio.no/isp/forskning/publikasjoner/nye-publikasjoner/gunnerud-ten-braak-reikeras-donolato---melby-lerva.html)

- Design: meta-analysis. Ages studied: 3 y to 18 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: In children, the overall bilingual advantage in executive function was very small and not robust, appearing mainly in particular subgroups.
- Limits: Summary recalled from memory; the paper was not re-read on the check date.
- Finding checked against: nothing; summarised from prior knowledge.

### `de-bruin-2015`

de Bruin, A., Treccani, B., & Della Sala, S. (2015). Cognitive advantage in bilingualism: An example of publication bias? Psychological Science. [Link](https://iris.unitn.it/handle/11572/187289)

- Design: systematic-review. Ages studied: 3 y to 75 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Of 104 conference abstracts on bilingualism and executive control, 63% of those supporting a bilingual advantage were later published in journals, against 36% of those that did not support it.
- Limits: Read from the journal society's press release.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `hoff-2012`

Hoff, E., Core, C., Place, S., Rumiche, R., Señor, M., & Parra, M. (2012). Dual language exposure and early bilingual development. Journal of Child Language. [Link](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4323282)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 18 mo to 2 y 6 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Comparing high-income bilingual and monolingual children aged 1 year 10 months to 2 years 6 months, monolinguals were ahead on vocabulary and grammar in their one language, but the groups were comparable in total vocabulary across languages.
- Limits: Toddlers.
- Finding checked against: the paper's own abstract or text.

### `ferjan-ramirez-2017`

Ferjan Ramírez, N., & Kuhl, P. (2017). Bilingual baby: Foreign language intervention in Madrid's infant education centers. Mind, Brain, and Education. [Link](https://www.washington.edu/news/2017/07/17/bilingual-babies-study-shows-how-exposure-to-a-foreign-language-ignites-infants-learning/)

- Design: quasi-experiment. Ages studied: 7 mo to 2 y 10 mo. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: 280 children aged 7 to 33 months in Madrid centres received 18 weeks of daily English play sessions with tutors. They produced about 74 English words or phrases per child per hour against 13 in the comparison group, and kept the gain 18 weeks later.
- Limits: Read from a university press release. Very young children with intensive live exposure.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).

### `jaekel-2017`

Jaekel, N., Schurig, M., Florian, M., & Ritter, M. (2017). From early starters to late finishers? A longitudinal study of early foreign language learning in school. Language Learning. [Link](https://zendy.io/title/10.1111/lang.12242)

- Design: longitudinal. Ages studied: 6 y to 13 y. Weight: moderate.
- Finding: Among 5,130 students in 31 academic-track German schools, those who began English in grade 1 were ahead in reading and listening in grade 5, but by grade 7 those who began in grade 3 were ahead.
- Limits: Read from a university press release. Early lessons were at most 90 minutes a week.
- Finding checked against: a secondary summary (press release, database entry or review page).
